children: New Delhi, Nov. 16 -- Bengaluru and Mumbai: The TVS family dispute is now a formal legal claim.

Lakshmi Venu has formally sought to partition the TVS Group's joint family assets, sending a notice to her father and the group patriarch, Venu Srinivasan, and her brother Sudarshan Venu, a development that suggests the dispute at the storied business group is headed to court.
Lakshmi Venu's legal notice asks her father to discharge his fiduciary duties as head of the family and effect a fair and lawful partition, two executives privy to the development said.

Lakshmi has alleged that the group's beneficial interest has been concentrated in favour of her brother Sudarshan, to the exclusion of her lawful rights, and called it a breach of "law" and "trust", according to the first executive.
The legal notice gives Venu Srinivasan and Sudarshan Venu one week to respond.

"Every effort will be made to see this get settled within the coming days. If not, then like in everything in life, there are always courts for assistance," said C. Aryama Sundaram, senior Supreme Court lawyer, who is the counsel helping Lakshmi.
According to Sundaram, all property under the TVS Group is coparcenary property, or assets on which both the daughter and son have equal rights under the 2005 Hindu Succession Act amendment.

"Since the summer of 2025, she (Lakshmi) has made multiple efforts to ensure a fair and equitable distribution is made. However, all her efforts to reconcile the matter have failed. So, she has very patiently tried to settle this matter within the family, and she has not been quick to take a legal route," said Sundaram.

The first executive cited earlier said that the notice "sets out Dr Lakshmi's claim to her rightful share and seeks a formal partition. It allows every opportunity for this to be resolved without going to court. Dr Lakshmi has reiterated her preference for an amicable and equitable resolution."

"The assets for which Dr Lakshmi seeks partition include the family interests held through the VS Trust and other holding vehicles and structures. These encompass the businesses and assets allotted to the Venu Srinivasan branch under the 2020 larger TVS family arrangement, including interests in TVS Holdings, TVS Motor Co, TVS Credit Services and Sundaram-Clayton," the executive added.

The three listed entities, TVS Motor, TVS Holdings and Sundaram-Clayton, had a combined market capitalization of Rs.2.37 trillion at market close on Monday. Financial services company TVS Credit Services, on the other hand, is privately held.

The VS Trust owns all of these businesses, and Srinivasan is its sole trustee. The trust owns 66.55% of TVS Holdings, which in turn owns 56% of TVS Motor. It also owns 46.83% of Sundaram-Clayton, which had a market cap of Rs.2,411 crore.
Lakshmi directly owns just 0.82% of TVS Holdings and 0.75% of Sundaram-Clayton.

Sudarshan Venu, 37, is chairman and managing director of TVS Motor, managing director of TVS Holdings, and oversees the financial services businesses. Lakshmi Venu, 43, runs the much smaller die-casting business at Sundaram-Clayton.

In her legal notice, she based her claim on the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, reasoning that it gives her the right to a fair share of the family property and allows her to seek its division, according to the first executive. She also pointed to the equal rights of daughters recognized under Section 6 of the Act.
Lakshmi's case depends on one key point: the division of the larger TVS Group six years ago did not settle how assets would be shared within her father's branch of the family.

A 2020 settlement had split the 115-year-old TVS industrial group among the sons of founder T.V. Sundaram Iyengar. Later, an agreement in March 2024 dealt with brand usage and non-compete obligations, but not ownership, said the executive cited above.

"The MoU (memorandum of understanding) of March 2024 merely dealt with the TVS brand usage and non-compete obligations. That is how TVS Holdings described it to the stock exchanges. It did not divide ownership. There was no valuation, no negotiation on value and no consideration, in stark contrast with the MOFA (memorandum of family settlement of 2020)," said the executive.
"It is unfortunate that requests for an amicable settlement have not so far progressed in a meaningful and timely way," Mallika Srinivasan, Lakshmi's mother, said in a statement on Monday.

"As a mother, to me, a son and daughter are equal in every respect. I do believe that Lakshmi has a legitimate share of the family assets, not inequal to that of Sudarshan's. I reiterate that this is a matter to be settled, in the interests of all stakeholders, through transparent dialogue, with equity, clarity and amity. I sincerely hope that we can move forward constructively, with grace and dignity," she said.
An email sent to Lakshmi and Srinivasan seeking their comments went unanswered.

The tension first became public in March at Sundaram-Clayton. Lakshmi objected to the company secretary reporting to the finance chief of TVS Holdings, rather than to her. The board first accepted the company secretary's resignation, then reversed the decision within 72 hours. Mint was the first to report the development on 31 March.

"The 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act gives both girls and boys equal rights to a family's property. Lakshmi's claim is simple: She is seeking what the law provides," said Mrunalini Deshmukh, a Mumbai-based family and matrimonial lawyer, who backs gender justice and women's rights. "At the basic level, Lakshmi's claim is something which challenges a patriarchal mindset and is visibly very distasteful."

Lakshmi's notice comes at a sensitive time for Srinivasan. As vice-chairman of Tata Trusts, his crucial vote in September had helped N. Chandrasekaran secure a third term as Tata Sons chairman, despite resistance from Noel Tata, who chairs Tata Trusts.
